lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 3, what did you group under each heading of a fact text? (Facts that belong together.) Today: research a topic yourself and write a report.
Research starts with questions: "What do bats eat? Where do they sleep?" Then look in a few sources: books, a trusted website, an expert. Use more than one, and check that they agree.
Take notes: write only the key words, in your own words, not whole sentences. Then sort your notes into groups: each group becomes a section of your report.
Use your own words. Copying a writer's sentences and calling them yours is not fair. To use someone's exact words, put them in speech marks and say who said them.
A report has a title and an opening that says what it is about. It has sections with headings, facts, examples and new words explained. It has pictures with captions, and a conclusion.
Be exact. Not "bats eat bugs" but "bats eat moths, midges and beetles". Explain special words: "Bats are nocturnal: they are active at night."
End with a conclusion that sums up. Then list your sources, the books and websites you used, so that readers can check your facts.
Try it in the world: choose an animal from your world, and find three facts about the real one in a book. Build an information board with headings in your village. Next: write a narrative.

exercises.prompt: What should you do before you start your research?
exercises.hint: What do you want to find out?
exercises.explain: Questions tell you what to look for: "What do bats eat? Where do they sleep?"
choices: write the questions you want to answer

exercises.prompt: Which is the best way to take notes?
exercises.hint: Notes are short.
exercises.explain: Good notes are key words in your own words: quick to write and easy to sort.
choices: key words, in your own words

exercises.prompt: A report should have headings that tell what each section is about.
exercises.hint: How do readers find what they need?
exercises.explain: True: headings help readers find each part.

exercises.prompt: Which is a heading for a report about bats?
exercises.hint: A heading names what a section is about.
exercises.explain: "What Bats Eat" tells readers what that section is about.

exercises.prompt: Where do you list the books and websites you used?
exercises.hint: Readers may want to check your facts.
exercises.explain: A list of sources at the end shows where your facts came from.
choices: in a list of sources at the end

exercises.prompt: Sort Zara's notes about bats into two sections.
exercises.hint: Is it something bats eat, or somewhere they live?
exercises.explain: Food: moths, midges and beetles. Homes: caves, old barns and hollow trees.

exercises.prompt: Put the parts of a report in order.
exercises.hint: What does the reader see first, and what comes at the very end?
exercises.explain: The title, the opening, sections with headings, the conclusion, then the list of sources.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence explains a special word?
exercises.hint: Look for a word and what it means.
exercises.explain: It explains nocturnal: active at night.
choices: Bats are nocturnal: they are active at night.

exercises.prompt: It is fine to copy whole paragraphs from a book and call them your own.
exercises.hint: Whose words are they?
exercises.explain: False: use your own words. To use a writer's exact words, put them in speech marks and name the writer.

exercises.prompt: Why use more than one source?
exercises.hint: What if one book has a mistake?
exercises.explain: Two or three sources that agree make you surer that the facts are right.
choices: to check that the facts agree

exercises.prompt: Which is the most exact sentence?
exercises.hint: Which one names exactly what bats eat?
exercises.explain: It names the exact food: much more useful than "stuff".
choices: Bats eat moths, midges and beetles.

exercises.prompt: Match each part of a report to what it is.
exercises.hint: Where does each one appear in a report?
exercises.explain: A caption goes under a picture, a heading names a section, a glossary explains special words, and a source is where a fact came from.

exercises.prompt: Zara uses the exact words of a bat expert. What must she do?
exercises.hint: How will readers know whose words they are?
exercises.explain: Speech marks show that they are someone else's exact words, and naming the expert gives the credit.
choices: put them in speech marks and name the expert
say they are her own words
change one word and keep them

exercises.prompt: Two books disagree about how long a bat lives. What should Bram do?
exercises.hint: How can you find out which book is right?
exercises.explain: A third trusted source can show which fact is right.
choices: check a third source he can trust

exercises.prompt: Which is the best conclusion for a report about bats?
exercises.hint: A conclusion sums up the report's main idea.
exercises.explain: It sums up what the report showed about bats.
choices: Bats are clever night hunters, worth protecting.
Once upon a time, there was a bat.

exercises.prompt: Every website is a trusted source.
exercises.hint: Who wrote it, and why?
exercises.explain: False: check who wrote a website and why. Museums, zoos and science groups are more trusted than a random page.

exercises.prompt: The source says: "Bats rest by day in dark roosts, such as caves and roof spaces." Which is the best note?
exercises.hint: A note is short, with only the key words.
exercises.explain: "rest by day: caves, roofs" keeps the key facts in a few words of your own.
choices: Bats rest by day in dark roosts, such as caves.

exercises.prompt: Put the steps of a research project in order.
exercises.hint: You cannot sort your notes before you take them.
exercises.explain: Questions, sources, notes, sorting, then writing.

exercises.prompt: Match each note about bats to its section heading.
exercises.hint: Ask which question each note answers: what, where, when or how?
exercises.explain: Moths and beetles: What Bats Eat. Caves and barns: Where Bats Live. Active at night: When Bats Are Busy. Using echoes: How Bats Find Food.

exercises.prompt: Sort them: a trusted source for bat facts, or not?
items: a book by a bat scientist
an advert for a bat toy
exercises.hint: Who made it, and do they know about bats, or do they want to sell you something?
exercises.explain: Trusted: a bat scientist's book, a zoo's website and a bat expert. Not trusted: a joke page and an advert, which are made to amuse or to sell.
